title: Not even "uff"
hookLine: don't say even uff to your parents, and lower the wing of humility to them (17:23–24)

cards: Your mother asks you, for the third time this week, how to send a photo on her phone. You show her.
And somewhere in the showing, before you've decided to, a small sound escapes: a breath out through the nose, a tiny sigh that means: this again. In Arabic it's uff.
And Surah seventeen, in a passage of commands about how to live, names that exact sound and rules it out.

teach.b: The passage begins: your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and kindness to parents. Notice the order: right after God come the people who raised you.
Then the scene narrows to old age, when one or both of them live with you and need you. In Pickthall's translation: "say not 'Fie' unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word."
Fie is his old English for uff.
Commentators point out that uff is about the smallest sound of annoyance there is. If the smallest is ruled out, everything bigger is too.
Then verse twenty-four gives a picture: lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy, like a bird lowering its wings over its chicks. Once, your parents did that for you. Now the wings are yours.

And the verse gives words to say: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." The name for all this is birr al-walidayn. Birr is a wide word: goodness, devotion, dutiful kindness.
Walidayn means the two parents. A hadith in Bukhari tells of a man who asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ who most deserves his good company.
Your mother, he said. Then who? Your mother.
Then who? Your mother. Then who?
Your father. The verse doesn't say parents are always right.

teach.h: SPEAK UNTO THEM A GRACIOUS WORD.
teach.b: Another verse, 31:15, says not to obey parents who push you to set partners beside God, and still to keep company with them kindly in this world. Gentleness even then, and it begins with the smallest sound.

how: Muslims treat kindness to parents as a major duty, especially in their old age; the prayer of 17:24 is often said for parents after the daily prayers, and keep praying for them after they die.

o: goodness to both parents, down to the smallest sigh
obeying your parents in everything, without question
the reward parents earn for raising their children

games.q: inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: the verse comes right after the command to worship God alone
17:23 joins the two: worship none but Him, and kindness to parents.
birr al-walidayn means obeying parents even in wrongdoing
31:15: don't obey them in wrongdoing against God, yet keep company with them kindly.
in Bukhari's hadith, the father is named first
the mother is named three times, then the father.

games.q: a man asks the Prophet who most deserves his good company. the Prophet says: your mother. then who?
games.why: your mother, again, and a third time, and only then your father (Bukhari).

practice: Bring one parent to mind, or someone who did a parent's work for you, a grandparent, an aunt, a foster parent; if they've died, this is for them too.
Remember one ordinary thing they did when you were small: a lunch packed, a ride home, a hand on your forehead.
If you pray, say the verse's own words for them: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they cared for me when I was little.

wordCard.voice: Birr al-walidayn. Goodness to the two parents, placed right after the worship of God, down to the smallest sigh. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: goodness to the two parents. walidayn is the dual: both parents.

carryVoice: Your line: not even a sigh. The wings are yours now. Day four hundred fifty-eight, done.
